title: Inversion
quote: All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there.
definition: Instead of asking how to achieve a goal, ask how you could guarantee failure — then avoid those things. Solving the inverse of a problem often reveals the answer the forward approach hides.
example: To build a great career, list everything that reliably destroys careers — dishonesty, burning bridges, never updating skills — and systematically avoid each one.
whenToUse: When a goal feels vague or overwhelming, flip it: what would guarantee the worst outcome?
trap: Forward-only thinking that ignores obvious, avoidable failure modes.

drill.scenario: A founder wants their startup to succeed. Which is the most Munger-like first move?
options: Write a vision statement about winning
List the top ways startups predictably die, and avoid them
drill.explanation: Inversion: identify guaranteed failure modes (running out of cash, no product-market fit, co-founder conflict) and design to avoid them.

title: Incentive-Caused Bias
quote: Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome.
definition: People (often unconsciously) rationalize behavior that serves their incentives. To predict behavior, study the incentives — not the stated intentions.
example: A salesperson paid on commission will, on average, recommend the product that pays them most — usually while sincerely believing it's best for you.
whenToUse: Any time you receive advice, evaluate a forecast, or design a system that rewards people.
trap: Trusting stated motives while ignoring the financial or social rewards shaping them.

drill.scenario: A fund manager insists their high-fee product is best for you. What should you weigh most?
drill.explanation: Incentive-caused bias predicts that compensation structure shapes the recommendation more than sincerity does.

title: Social Proof
quote: Big-shot businessmen get into these waves of social proof.
definition: We copy the behavior of others, especially under uncertainty or stress. It's efficient in stable environments and disastrous in bubbles and panics.
example: An investor buys a soaring stock simply because everyone else is — confusing the crowd's enthusiasm for analysis.
whenToUse: When you notice you're doing something mainly because others are.
trap: Outsourcing judgment to the crowd at exactly the moment the crowd is wrong.

drill.scenario: Everyone in your circle is buying one hot asset. The Munger move is to:
options: Buy more than them to keep up
Pause and reason independently from fundamentals
Buy a little to fit in
Trust that so many people can't be wrong
drill.explanation: Social proof is strongest under uncertainty. Independent reasoning is the antidote.

title: Confirmation Bias
quote: The human mind is a lot like the human egg... it shuts out all other sperm.
definition: Once we hold a conclusion, we seek confirming evidence and dismiss disconfirming evidence. Beliefs harden regardless of truth.
example: After picking a stock, you read only bullish articles and explain away every warning sign.
whenToUse: Whenever you feel certain — deliberately hunt for the strongest opposing case.
trap: Mistaking a one-sided evidence pile for a balanced analysis.

drill.scenario: You're convinced a decision is right. The best disconfirming habit is to:
options: Articulate the strongest case against your own view
Move faster before doubt creeps in
Ask people who already agree with you
drill.explanation: Munger insisted you can't hold an opinion until you can argue the other side better than its proponents.

title: Circle of Competence
quote: Knowing what you don't know is more useful than being brilliant.
definition: Operate within the domains you genuinely understand. The boundary matters more than the size — knowing where your competence ends prevents costly errors.
example: Buffett and Munger avoided tech for decades, not because it was bad, but because it sat outside their circle.
whenToUse: Before any consequential decision: 'Do I actually understand this, or do I just feel like I do?'
trap: Overconfidence that pushes you to act outside what you truly know.

drill.scenario: You're offered a deal in an industry you barely understand. The disciplined response is:
options: Decline or invest the time to genuinely understand it first
Follow what experts on TV say
drill.explanation: Staying inside your circle of competence — or honestly expanding it before acting — beats faking understanding.

title: Compounding
quote: The first rule of compounding: never interrupt it unnecessarily.
definition: Small advantages, repeated over long periods, produce nonlinear results. This applies to money, knowledge, and relationships alike.
example: Reading 30 minutes a day seems trivial daily, but compounds into a vast knowledge advantage over decades.
whenToUse: When evaluating anything long-term — savings, habits, skill-building.
trap: Underestimating the long-run payoff of consistent small actions, and interrupting compounding for short-term gains.

drill.scenario: Which best reflects Munger's view of compounding?
options: Protect consistent long-run growth and avoid interrupting it
Trade frequently to capture every move
drill.explanation: Compounding rewards patience and continuity; needless interruption (taxes, fees, churn) is its enemy.

title: Margin of Safety
quote: Engineering has a margin of safety. Life should too.
definition: Build in a buffer against error, bad luck, and the limits of your own knowledge. Borrowed from engineering, where bridges are built to hold far more than expected load.
example: Buying an asset worth $1 for $0.60 leaves room to be wrong about the valuation and still come out fine.
whenToUse: Whenever outcomes are uncertain and downside is real — finance, planning, risk.
trap: Operating with no buffer, so a single error or surprise is catastrophic.

drill.scenario: An investment looks great only if everything goes perfectly. Munger would say:
options: Go all in, it's a sure thing
Demand a margin of safety so you survive being wrong
drill.explanation: A margin of safety protects you precisely because the future is uncertain and you will sometimes be wrong.

title: Ecosystem & Competition
quote: You may see displacement... like ecosystems where a species fills a niche.
definition: Businesses and ideas compete like organisms in an ecosystem — niches, specialization, and survival pressures. Borrowing from biology clarifies competitive dynamics.
example: A specialist company dominating a narrow niche can out-survive a generalist, much like a specialized species in a stable habitat.
whenToUse: When analyzing competition, market structure, or why some players persist.
trap: Treating markets as static rather than as evolving, competitive ecosystems.

drill.scenario: Why might a small niche company beat a large generalist?
options: It occupies a defensible niche with specialized advantages
drill.explanation: Ecosystem thinking: specialization in a defensible niche can outcompete broad but shallow generalists.

title: Lollapalooza Effect
quote: Really big effects... only happen when factors combine.
definition: When several psychological tendencies or forces act in the same direction at once, they don't add — they multiply, producing extreme outcomes.
example: An auction combines social proof, scarcity, commitment, and reciprocity — together driving people to wildly overpay.
whenToUse: When an outcome seems extreme; look for multiple biases stacking together.
trap: Analyzing one factor at a time and missing the compounding interaction of several.

drill.scenario: An outcome is far more extreme than any single cause explains. Munger suspects:
options: Several forces combining and multiplying — a Lollapalooza
drill.explanation: The Lollapalooza effect describes multiple tendencies converging to produce outsized results.

title: Availability Misweighing
quote: The mind overweighs what's easily available.
definition: We judge likelihood and importance by what comes to mind easily — recent, vivid, or emotional events — rather than by actual frequency.
example: After seeing news of a plane crash, people overestimate flying risk though driving is far more dangerous.
whenToUse: When estimating risk or probability, ask whether vividness is distorting your sense of the odds.
trap: Confusing how easily something is recalled with how likely or important it actually is.

drill.scenario: A dramatic recent event makes a rare risk feel huge. The corrective is to:
options: Trust the gut feeling of danger
Check actual base rates and frequencies
drill.explanation: Availability bias is countered by consulting real base rates rather than vivid memories.
